section.title: What is a CSS box?
section.p: A CSS box is the area layout creates to place an element and its content on a page. It is not an XML tag and does not have to be drawn with a visible border. CSS uses the element’s display value to decide whether it generates a box. Usually an element generates one box, but some display values generate none or more than one. See CSS Display 3, Box generation.

The XML element is the source that CSS selects. The box is the area that layout sizes and positions. The box’s content area holds text, child boxes, images or other content. Around it, CSS can add padding, a border and margin:

ul.li: Content is the text or other content inside the box.
Padding is space between the content and the border.
Border is the edge around the padding. It is visible when border styling gives it a visible style.
Margin is space outside the border, between this box and surrounding boxes.

section.p: These areas may have zero size. Their relationship is defined by CSS Box Model 4 §2, The CSS Box Model. Sizing properties set the content area’s dimensions, with box-sizing choosing whether the declared size measures the content box or border box. Margin and padding properties set the corresponding outer and inner spaces.
The properties described here also accept the CSS-wide keywords. See Inheritance and default values.

The containing block is the reference box used to calculate some sizes and percentages. It is often formed by an ancestor box. Its inline size is the size along the text line. In horizontal writing, that is usually the width. See CSS Display 3, Containing Blocks and CSS Writing Modes 4, Abstract Box Terminology.

section.title: Units in size and spacing values
section.p: CSS Values 4 §5.5, Percentages; CSS Values 4 §6, Distance Units.

A length is a number followed by a unit, such as 12pt or 1em. The unit tells CSS how to interpret the number. A percentage, such as 60%, is a different kind of value: it means a fraction of a reference size. Which size it refers to depends on the property. For the sizing properties below, it is generally a corresponding size of the containing block; for margins and padding, it is based on the containing block’s inline size.
Common length units used in this guide are:

row.entry: Font-relative length based on the selected element’s font size.
Font-relative length based on the root element’s font size.

ul.li: For example, padding: 12pt sets twelve points of padding on each side. margin-block: 1em sets a margin based on the element’s font size. The same 1em can therefore represent different lengths on elements with different font sizes.
60% is not a length unit; it scales with the property’s percentage reference size.
CSS also defines other font-relative, viewport-relative and container-relative length units. See CSS Values 4 §6, Distance Units for the full list and definitions.
A zero length may be written as 0 without a unit; nonzero lengths need a unit. The allowed range depends on the property. For example, margins may be negative, but padding cannot.

section.title: Choose what a size measures
section.p: CSS Sizing 3 §3, Specifying Box Sizes.
box-sizing determines whether a fixed size measures the content box or the border box.

ul.li: content-box measures the content area. Padding and border are added outside the specified size.
border-box measures through the outside border edge. The content area is reduced to make room for padding and border.

section.p: The initial value is content-box .

Here, the content area is 12em wide. The padding adds 1em on each inline side, and the border adds another 1px on each side. Change box-sizing to border-box to keep the total border-edge size at 12em; the content area becomes narrower to make room for the padding and border. The padding and border declarations make the edges visible in this example.
Preferred width, height, minimum and maximum dimensions are covered in Box dimensions.

section.title: Set margins outside the border
section.p: CSS Box Model 4 §3, Margins; CSS Logical Properties 1 §4.2, Flow-Relative Margins.
margin-top , margin-right , margin-bottom and margin-left set the space outside each physical side of the border.

Each accepts a length such as 12pt, a percentage such as 5%, auto, or anchor-size() . Negative lengths and percentages are allowed. A percentage is calculated from the inline size of the containing block, including for top and bottom margins. auto lets the layout algorithm distribute available space according to the formatting context.

anchor-size() accepts an optional anchor name, an optional size keyword, or both, followed by an optional length or percentage fallback. The size keyword can be width, height, block, inline, self-block or self-inline. The fallback is used when the anchor cannot be resolved.
Each physical margin longhand starts at 0.
Adjacent block margins can collapse into one margin. Their used separation is not always the sum of both values.

margin sets one to four physical side values. One value applies to all sides. Two values set top and bottom, then left and right. Three set top, left and right, then bottom. Four set top, right, bottom and left, clockwise from the top. Its initial value is 0.

In this declaration, the section has 1em of margin above and below it, and 2em to its left and right. Replace section with the name of an element in your XML. The shorthand changes the space outside the border; it does not add space between the content and the border.

margin-block-start and margin-block-end set margins at the start and end of the block axis. margin-inline-start and margin-inline-end set margins at the start and end of the inline axis. Their sides follow writing-mode and direction.

margin-block sets the block-start and block-end margins. margin-inline sets the inline-start and inline-end margins. With one value both sides are equal; with two, the first sets the start side and the second the end side.

The four logical longhands accept the same values as the physical margin properties and start at 0. Each logical shorthand accepts one or two values from that same grammar. The shorthand’s initial values come from its longhands, each of which starts at 0.
For example, a step element can have different spacing before and after it, and equal spacing at both inline sides:

margin-block gives each step 0.5em at block-start and 1em at block-end. margin-inline gives it 1em at both inline sides. In the usual horizontal, left-to-right writing mode, these are top, bottom, left and right respectively. In another writing mode or direction, the logical sides follow that mode instead of staying tied to the same physical edges. Replace step with the element name used for your procedure steps.
margin-trim removes in-flow child margins that touch the corresponding edge of a container.
Its initial value is none .

ul.li: none does not trim margins. Normal margin collapsing can still occur.
block trims block-start and block-end margins at the container’s edges.
inline trims inline-start and inline-end margins.
block-start , block-end , inline-start and inline-end select individual edges.

section.p: You can combine block with inline, or combine individual edge keywords with one another. Do not mix these two groups in one value. The property applies to block, multi-column, flex and grid containers.
margin-break controls the box’s block-axis margins where they adjoin a page or column break. See CSS Fragmentation 4 §5.2.

ul.li: auto is the initial value. At an unforced break, margins adjoining the break are limited to the remaining space before the break and become zero after it. At a forced break, margins before the break are truncated, while margins after it are preserved. Cloned margins are always truncated to zero.
keep preserves margins adjoining the break.
discard truncates adjoining margins, including at the beginning and end of a fragmentation context.

section.title: Set padding inside the border
section.p: CSS Box Model 4 §4, Padding; CSS Logical Properties 1 §4.4, Flow-Relative Padding.
padding-top , padding-right , padding-bottom and padding-left set the space between the content and the corresponding border edge.

Each accepts a non-negative length, such as 12pt, or percentage, such as 5%. A percentage is calculated from the inline size of the containing block, including for top and bottom padding. Padding cannot be negative.
Physical and logical padding longhands and shorthands have an initial value of 0.

padding sets one to four physical side values using the same top, right, bottom, left order as margin. One value applies to all sides; two set vertical then horizontal sides; three set top, horizontal sides, then bottom; four set each side clockwise.
For example, a warning element can have more room inside its border at the top and bottom than at the sides:

The first value adds 1em above and below the content. The second adds 1.5em to the left and right. Padding is inside the border, unlike margin. Replace warning with the element name used for this kind of message in your XML.
padding-block-start and padding-block-end set padding at the start and end of the block axis. padding-inline-start and padding-inline-end set padding at the start and end of the inline axis.

padding-block sets both block-axis sides. padding-inline sets both inline-axis sides. One value applies to both sides; two values set the start side followed by the end side. The physical sides change with the writing mode and text direction.
Each logical padding longhand uses the same non-negative length-percentage values as the physical padding properties. Each logical shorthand accepts one or two values from the same grammar.
Use logical padding when the spacing should follow the text direction. In this example, padding-inline-start adds space at the beginning of the text line:

The block padding adds 0.5em at both ends of the block axis. The inline-start padding adds 1em before the text begins. In a right-to-left writing direction, inline-start is on the right. Replace definition with the element name used for this content in your XML.
